doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in northern England
title: The eleven-year-old rhythm club
summary: She was in a rhythm club at eleven, strictly devoted to King Oliver and Morton and nothing after 1929, and opposed to needing written music.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: You anticipated my next question. Were you kind of a club of one?

No. As a matter of fact we had a rhythm club, and I was eleven years old at the time, and I can remember asking someone just quite recently when Bobby and I were up in the north of England. I said, “Tell me, what was I like when I was eleven?” And this woman said, “You were a cheeky little monkey.” I wanted to know everything. For instance we were very square, as jazz fans, and we liked the older type music. We liked King Oliver and we liked Jelly Roll Morton, and I didn’t subscribe to the idea of anyone needing music. I thought real jazz, you didn’t need music. So that has been a battle royal between Bobby and me all these years. I didn’t see the sense in that and it was all too glib or too clever. I wanted to have that wonderful ensemble playing that you had in the King Oliver band with all these horns all playing away, and that wonderful spirit, but not have it strained, that purity of it by sort of having to learn too much about it. I equated that. And so we had rather an active rhythm club, but it was very square. I don’t think we branched out beyond 1929. I think probably “Weatherbird” was probably as late as we went with that recording.
